title: Breakout
summary: Paddle, ball, and a wall of bricks — but the Frame lesson is a mechanism the other games don't use: enter-arguments. When the ball launches, the transition carries the velocity into the target state (`-> (vx, vy) $InFlight`), where a `$>(vx, vy)` handler seeds the ball's state-local velocity. The ball is its own sub-machine; the brick field its own system.
teaches: Enter-arguments threaded through a transition into a state's $>(params) · a Ball sub-machine (attached → in-flight → lost/respawn) · a BrickField system · push$/pop$ pause
controls: A/D or ←/→ move paddle · hold to aim · SPACE launch · P pause · SPACE start · R restart

machines.title: Breakout — the game flow
machines.blurb: $Attract → $Playing → $LevelClear / $GameOver, with pause as a push$/pop$ interrupt. Owns the Ball and BrickField children; routes paddle/wall/brick events to them and reads their state back. $LevelClear's $>() bumps the level, then re-racks the wall and re-attaches the ball for the next round.

machines.title: Ball — a sub-machine with enter-arguments
machines.blurb: $AttachedToPaddle → $InFlight → $Lost → back to attached. The launch is the showcase: `launch(vx, vy) { -> (vx, vy) $InFlight }` — the transition carries the velocity as enter-arguments into $InFlight's `$>(vx, vy)` handler, which seeds the state-local $.vx/$.vy. $Lost runs a 2-second respawn timer the scene reads as a fade-in.

machines.title: BrickField — the wall
machines.blurb: A single $Active state over a list of bricks. break_brick(i) knocks one out and decrements the count; is_cleared() drives the orchestrator's $LevelClear transition. The scene owns brick geometry and collision; the field owns which bricks survive.
